title: Review an async method that blocks on .Result
description: Problem: Review an async method that blocks on .Result. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: A developer writes an async method that calls another async method but blocks on it with .Result or .Wait() to get a synchronous return value. In a console app or background service, this can cause deadlocks, thread pool starvation, and unresponsive applications. In ASP.NET Classic, it deadlocks the request thread. In ASP.NET Core, it causes thread pool exhaustion under load. The code compiles, passes unit tests, and fails in production.

items: Understand the async await state machine and how it schedules work on the thread pool
Learn why blocking on async code causes deadlocks in synchronization context environments
Identify thread pool starvation symptoms: high CPU, slow responses, and unresponsive endpoints
Apply async all the way: propagate async signatures from top to bottom

terms.definition: A context that controls where continuations run. ASP.NET Classic uses a request context that allows only one thread at a time.
A state where two or more threads are blocked forever, each waiting for the other to release a resource.
A condition where all thread pool threads are blocked, preventing the runtime from processing queued work items.
A design principle where async methods call other async methods without blocking, keeping the call chain asynchronous from entry point to IO.

data.text: Blocking on async code defeats the purpose of async IO. Instead of freeing threads to serve other requests, the thread sits idle waiting for an operation to complete. Under light load, the application appears to work. Under production load, thread pool starvation causes requests to queue, latency spikes, and eventually timeouts. The fix is simple: make the calling method async and await the operation.

data.title: .Result and .Wait() are not free
data.text: Blocking on async code holds a thread for the entire duration of the IO operation. In a server environment, that thread cannot serve another request. The cost is not visible in a single-user test but explodes under concurrent load.

The problematic code calls an async method from a synchronous method using .Result. The async method needs to resume on the original context, but the original context is blocked waiting for the result. The two threads wait for each other forever: the classic deadlock.

data.text: The correct approach is to make the calling method async and propagate the async signature all the way up the call stack. If you cannot make the entry point async, use .GetAwaiter().GetResult() only as a last resort in console applications where no synchronization context exists. In ASP.NET Core, always prefer async all the way.

data.title: Limited acceptable scenarios
items: Console application Main method: no synchronization context exists, so .GetAwaiter().GetResult() is safe
Top-level statements in .NET 6+: the entry point can be async directly
Legacy code boundaries where you cannot change the signature: wrap the call in Task.Run and accept the thread pool cost
Unit tests that need to call async methods: use async test methods instead of blocking

data.title: ConfigureAwait in libraries
data.text: Library code should use ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid capturing the synchronization context. This prevents deadlocks when the library is consumed by UI or ASP.NET Classic applications. ASP.NET Core does not have a synchronization context, so ConfigureAwait(false) is optional but still a good practice.

items.question: Does ASP.NET Core have a synchronization context?
items.answer: No. ASP.NET Core removed the synchronization context to improve scalability. Blocking with .Result does not deadlock, but it still blocks a thread and causes thread pool starvation under load.

items.question: What is the difference between .Result and .Wait()?
items.answer: .Result blocks the thread and returns the result or throws an AggregateException wrapping the original. .Wait() blocks the thread and returns only a bool or throws AggregateException. Both are bad in async code.

items.question: Can I use .GetAwaiter().GetResult() in ASP.NET Core?
items.answer: It will not deadlock because there is no synchronization context. However, it still blocks a thread and hurts scalability. Use async all the way instead.

items.question: What is thread pool starvation?
items.answer: When all available thread pool threads are blocked, the runtime cannot process new work items. Requests queue up, latency increases, and the application becomes unresponsive until threads are released.

data.title: Eliminate blocking calls
data.description: Refactor a codebase that uses .Result and .Wait() to use async all the way.
steps: Search the codebase for .Result and .Wait() calls on Task types
For each call, make the containing method async and await the operation
Update the method signature and all callers up to the entry point
Run a load test before and after to measure thread pool usage and request latency
Add a code analysis rule to block new .Result and .Wait() calls
data.expectedOutcome: No .Result or .Wait() calls remain on Task types. The application handles concurrent load with fewer threads and lower latency.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Blocking on async code wastes threads and causes deadlocks or starvation
Async all the way is the only scalable pattern for server applications
Use ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries to avoid synchronization context issues
Treat .Result and .Wait() as code smells in any async codebase
data.takeaway: Async code is contagious. If one method blocks, the whole chain suffers.
